t.7.1: Then, during the waxing of the lord of herbs, the moon, and on a lunar day endowed with the virtue of an auspicious seventh house, Himavān, with his kinsmen gathered around him, performed the rite of the marriage consecration for his daughter.
t.7.2: With the auspicious preparations for the wedding, the women in every house were busy, and out of affection for the Mountain, his city and his inner palace could be likened to a single family.
t.7.3: That city, its great highways strewn with saṃtānaka flowers and its rows of banners fashioned from Chinese silk, blazing with the radiance of its golden archways, shone forth like heaven transported to another place.
t.7.4: Though there was a whole line of sons, Umā, as if she were their only child, as if seen after a long absence, as if risen from the dead, became for her parents a special source of joy, because her marriage was near.
t.7.5: With blessings spoken over her, she passed from lap to lap and enjoyed one ornament after another; the affection of the Mountain's family, though divided among its many kin, came to rest in her as its one abode.
t.7.6: At the auspicious hour sacred to Mitra, when the Uttaraphalgunī stars had come into conjunction with the hare-marked moon, the women of her kin who had husbands and sons living performed the adornment of her body.
t.7.7: She graced the attire for the ceremonial anointing: its color set off by tender shoots of dūrvā grass studded with white mustard seeds, with a silk garment worn below the navel, and with an arrow held in hand.
t.7.8: And the girl, coming into contact with the new arrow used in the rite of consecration, shone like the slender crescent of the moon being kindled by the ray of the sun at the close of the dark fortnight.
t.7.9: The women led her toward the four-pillared pavilion, the oil on her body rubbed away with lodhra paste, her limbs tinted with kāleya paste now half-dried, and wearing a garment fit for the ceremonial bath.
t.7.10: On this floor laid with slabs of beryl and adorned with patterns of unpierced pearls, the women tipped water from golden pitchers and bathed her to the sound of music.
t.7.11: She, her limbs made pure by the auspicious bath and wearing the garment fit for going forth to meet her husband, shone like the earth when the bathing of the rain-cloud's waters has ended and the kāśa grass stands in full bloom.
t.7.12: And from that place, held by devoted wives, she was led to the middle of the wedding altar, which had a canopy, was fitted with four jewelled pillars, and held a seat already prepared.
t.7.13: Having seated the slender maiden there facing east, the women sitting before her lingered for a moment, their eyes captivated by her true, natural beauty, even though the adornments lay ready at hand.
t.7.14: One woman took the ends of her hair, which the warmth of incense smoke had made to give up their dampness, and, with flowers set within, bound them into a splendid knot, winding it round with a garland of pale madhūka blossoms interwoven with dūrvā grass.
t.7.15: They made her body one on which white aguru paste was laid and leaf-patterns were traced in gorocanā; and she stood there, surpassing the loveliness of the Trisrotas, whose sandbanks are marked with cakravāka birds.
t.7.17: A sprout of young barley, set behind her ear, rested upon her cheek, roughened by the astringent lodhra powder and made deeply golden with a smear of gorocanā; and by the contrast it gained there, it held fast the eyes of all who looked.
t.7.16: Surpassing both the lotus with a bee clinging to it and the moon's disc crossed by a streak of cloud, the beauty of her face, framed by its well-arranged curls, cut short all talk of comparison.
t.7.18: And the lower lip of that shapely-limbed maiden, divided by its fine line, its redness lightly rubbed with beeswax, the fruit of its loveliness now close at hand, took on through its quiverings a certain indescribable charm.
t.7.20: Seeing her eyes, lovely as the petals of a fine blue lotus, the women adorning her took up the black collyrium not with any thought of heightening the beauty of those eyes, but only because it was auspicious.
t.7.19: Her friend dyed her feet and teasingly blessed her, saying, “With this foot touch the crescent moon on your husband's head!” Without a word, she struck her friend with a garland.
t.7.21: As the ornaments were being put on her, she shone like a creeper with flowers springing forth, like the night with stars rising, like a river with birds alighting upon it.
t.7.22: And having beheld herself shining in the image of the mirror, she of the long, steady eyes grew eager to go to Hara; for the fruit of women's adornment is to be seen by the beloved.
t.7.23: Then her mother, taking up with two fingers moist, auspicious yellow orpiment and red arsenic, lifted up her face, at whose ears hung spotless ivory leaf-ornaments.
t.7.24: The first wish that had grown in her along with the budding of Umā's breasts, that very wish Menā somehow fulfilled as she marked her daughter's brow with the tilaka of the wedding consecration.
t.7.26: Clad in fresh linen silk and holding a new mirror, she shone all the more, like the shore of the Milk Ocean heaped with foam, or like an autumn night with the full moon.
t.7.25: And she, her eyes clouded with tears, tied upon her daughter's hand the woollen wedding thread, which was set in place at another spot on the arm as the nurse's fingers pushed it along.
t.7.28: "May you win your husband's unbroken love," the women said to Umā as she bowed before them; yet she, who was to share half of his very body, left behind even the blessings of those who loved her.
t.7.27: Her mother, expert in all that had to be done, made her, the very foundation of the family, bow down to the family deities, who had first been worshipped, and then had her touch, one after another, the feet of the virtuous matrons.
t.7.29: Having completed every rite for her in keeping with both his wishes and his wealth, the accomplished Mountain, gracious in the assembly, remained in the hall where his friends were gathered, awaiting the arrival of Vṛṣāṅka, the Bull-bannered god.
t.7.30: Meanwhile, on Kubera's mountain, the Mothers, full of reverent care, set before the Chastiser of the Cities, the bridegroom too, an adornment befitting that marriage, his first taking of a bride's hand.
t.7.31: Out of regard for them, that splendor of auspicious wedding adornment was merely touched by Īśvara; for the very garb of that all-pervading lord passed into another form, one befitting a bridegroom.
t.7.32: The ash itself became his white body-unguent, the skull itself the splendor of a spotless crest-jewel, and the very elephant hide took on the nature of a silken garment, marked with yellow rocanā along its borders.
t.7.33: That eye of his which shone between his temples, with a clear tawny pupil set within it, itself became, by its very presence there, the tilaka mark that would otherwise be drawn in yellow orpiment.
t.7.34: Of the lords of serpents, who were about to become other ornaments, each according to its place on the body, only their bodies underwent a change; the splendours of the jewels in their hoods remained just as they were.
t.7.35: Even by day the moon spat forth the splendour of its rays, and being young it did not yet show its mark. Since Hara's crest was always lit by that moon, what need had he to put on a crest-jewel?
t.7.36: Thus he, the sole source of marvels, who by his own power had brought about the customary rite of adornment, beheld his own image reflected in a sword held up to him by the Gaṇas standing near.
t.7.37: Leaning on the arm of Nandin, he mounted the bull, whose broad back was spread with a tiger's skin and who, out of devotion to him, had shrunk his vast bulk, and, as though he had mounted Kailāsa itself, he set forth.
t.7.38: The Mothers, following that god, their ear-ornaments swaying with the jolting of their own mounts, made the sky seem a lotus pond with their faces, golden with the pollen of their haloes of light.
t.7.39: And behind those golden-radiant ones shone Kālī, adorned with skulls, like a line of dark rain-clouds flecked with cranes, with lightning flung far out ahead of it.
t.7.40: Then the sound of auspicious instruments, raised by the Trident-Bearer's gaṇas who went before him, rose up into the towering peaks of the celestial chariots and announced to the gods that the moment for service had come.
t.7.41: The thousand-rayed Sun held over him a new parasol fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, and he, his crest close beneath its silken fringe, shone as though the Gaṅgā were falling upon his head.
t.7.43: Behind him followed the first Ordainer, Brahmā, and the Supreme Person himself, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, with the cry of "Victory!", a voice that magnified his greatness as an oblation makes a fire blaze higher.
t.7.42: Then Gaṅgā and Yamunā, taking bodily form, attended the god with chowries in hand; though they had cast off their river-form, it was as though a flight of swans could still be seen with them.
t.7.44: That one single form was divided threefold, and among these three, being first or last is shared in common: at times Hara precedes Viṣṇu, at times Hari precedes him, at times Vedhas precedes them both, and at times those two stand before the Creator.
t.7.45: The guardians of the worlds, with Puruhūta at their head, their attire made humble by setting aside the insignia of their splendor, signaled to Nandin that they sought a glance from the Lord; presented by him, they bowed to Śiva with joined palms.
t.7.46: He honored the lotus-born god with a nod of his head, Hari with words, the slayer of Vṛtra with a smile, and all the other gods with a mere glance, each according to his rank.
t.7.47: When the Seven Sages offered him blessings of victory before him, he said to them with a smile: “In this wedding sacrifice now being performed, you have long since been chosen by me as the officiating adhvaryu priests.”
t.7.48: As skilled singers led by Viśvāvasu sang of his glorious feat against Tripura, he who wears a sliver of the lord of stars, untouched by the changes darkness brings, traversed the path.
t.7.49: His mount, moving playfully through the sky with tinkling golden bells, carried him, again and again tossing its horns, on which clouds were impaled, so that they seemed to have mud clinging to them from butting against riverbanks.
t.7.50: In a moment he reached the city guarded by the lord of mountains, a city never assailed by enemies, as though drawn forward by golden threads, the glances of Hara that had fastened upon it ahead.
t.7.51: Near that city the god, his throat dark blue as a rain cloud, gazed at out of curiosity by citizens with upturned faces, descended from the path marked by his own arrows and came to the nearby surface of the earth.
t.7.52: Delighted at his coming, the emperor of mountains went forth to meet him with herds of elephants mounted by his prosperous kinsmen, as though with his own slopes crowned with trees in full blossom.
t.7.53: At the gate of the city, whose doors had been thrown open, the two companies of the gods and of the mountains came together, their clamor spreading far, like two floods of water when the single dam dividing them has burst.
t.7.54: When Hara, whom the three worlds revere, bowed to him, the Mountain was abashed, for he did not realize that his own head had already been bent low by Hara's majesty.
t.7.56: At that moment, along the rows of mansions, the beautiful women of the city, eager to catch sight of Īśāna, abandoned all other tasks, and their actions were such as these.
t.7.55: He, the splendor of his face blossoming with joy, went ahead of his son-in-law and led him into the opulent mansion, whose market streets were strewn with flowers up to the ankles.
t.7.57: As one woman rushed suddenly toward the window, her mass of hair, which had shed its garland as it came undone, was for the moment not even thought of for binding, nor was it even held back with her hand.
t.7.58: One woman snatched away her forefoot, still wet with dye, from the grip of the maid adorning her, and, forgetting her graceful gait, laid down a trail marked with lac all the way to the window.
t.7.59: Another woman, having adorned her right eye with collyrium and leaving her left eye deprived of it, went just as she was to the window, still holding the applicator stick.
t.7.60: Another woman, her gaze sent out through the lattice window, did not tie the knot of her skirt that had come loose as she hurried out; she simply stood there clutching her garment with a hand whose jewelled ornaments cast their glow into her navel.
t.7.61: At that moment the girdle of a certain woman, only half-strung when she rose in haste, kept slipping apart at every faltering step, until nothing remained of it but the thread fastened at the base of her big toe.
t.7.62: Their openings filled with the faces of those women, intensely curious, faces laden with the fragrance of wine, whose restless eyes were like bees, the windows seemed as though adorned with thousand-petalled lotuses.
t.7.63: Meanwhile the moon-crested god reached the royal highway, crowded with banners and spanned by lofty arches, making the pinnacles of the palaces, even by day, shine with doubled splendour as if bathed in moonlight.
t.7.64: The women, drinking him in with their eyes, him who alone was worth beholding, turned to no other objects of sense; for indeed the workings of their remaining senses had, as it were, entered wholly into their eyes.
t.7.65: Fittingly indeed did Aparṇā, delicate though she was, practise for his sake austerity so hard to perform; the woman who might win even servitude to him would have her desires fulfilled, how much more one who gains a resting-place upon his lap!
t.7.66: Had this pair, whose beauty each finds desirable in the other, not been joined together, the effort of the Lord of Creatures in fashioning beauty in these two would have been in vain.
t.7.67: Surely the body of the flower-weaponed one was not burned by this one in mounting wrath; rather, I think, Kāma, on beholding this god, cast off his body of his own accord out of shame.
t.7.68: Friend, having by good fortune entered into kinship with this Lord, a bond long prayed for in his heart's desire, the king of mountains will now carry still higher his head, already lofty from bearing the earth.
t.7.69: Thus hearing the talk of the charming women of Oṣadhiprastha, so pleasant to the ear, the Three-eyed God reached the dwelling of Himālaya, where the handfuls of parched rice they scattered were crushed to powder by their armlets.
t.7.70: Alighting there from the bull, like the sun emerging from an autumn cloud, with Acyuta offering him his hand, he entered the inner courts of the Lord of Mountains, which Kamalāsana had entered before him.
t.7.71: Following him, the gods with Indra at their head, the supreme sages led by the Seven Ṛṣis, and the Gaṇas went to the Mountain's abode, just as the highest aims follow upon a praiseworthy undertaking.
t.7.72: There the Lord, seated on the guest's seat, duly accepted everything the Mountain brought him on a new silken cloth: the guest-water with jewels and the cow's curds mixed with honey, all of it accompanied by the proper mantras, with nothing done without them.
t.7.73: Clad in fine silk garments, he was led into the bride's presence by the well-mannered guards of the inner apartments, just as the ocean, its lines of foam gleaming, is drawn toward the shore by the fresh rays of the moon.
t.7.74: Joined with that maiden, the radiance of whose moon-like face had grown full, Śiva became like the world joined with autumn: the night-lotuses of his eyes burst into bloom, and the waters of his heart grew clear.
t.7.75: The eyes of the two, eager for one another yet timid whenever they chanced to meet, held steady for a moment and then drawn back, felt in that instant the restraint of shyness.
t.7.77: Umā's hair bristled with a thrill, and the Bull-bannered god's fingers grew moist with sweat; at the joining of their hands, it was as though the working of Manobhava had been divided equally between the two of them.
t.7.76: The Eight-formed One took her hand, with its copper-red fingers, offered to him by her father the Mountain, as though it were the first sprouting shoot of Smara, who in fear of him had hidden his body within the body of Umā.
t.7.78: Any other bride and groom who have performed the rite of taking hands gain supreme loveliness merely through the presence of these two; what, then, can be said of the splendor of that pair themselves at that moment?
t.7.79: As they walked in reverent circles, keeping the high-flaming fire to their right, that couple shone like day and night joined to each other, moving round the slopes of Meru.
t.7.80: Having led the couple three times around the fire, the family priest had the bride, whose eyes had closed at the touch of her husband's fingertips, cast parched grain into that brightly blazing flame.
t.7.81: At the instruction of the priest, she drew toward her face, with cupped hands, the sweet-smelling smoke of the parched-grain offering; and that smoke, its plume creeping along her cheek, became for a moment a blue lotus adorning her ear.
t.7.82: From taking in the smoke as the rite prescribed, the bride's face became thus: the curve of her cheeks slightly moist and flushed, the black collyrium of her eyes spreading, and her ear-ornament of barley shoots wilted.
t.7.83: The Brahmin said to the bride, "Child, this fire is the first witness of your marriage; together with Śiva, your husband, you must practise dharma, setting aside all hesitation."
t.7.84: That speech of her guru was drunk in by Bhavānī, her ears stretched wide to the corners of her eyes, just as the first water of Indra's rains is drunk by the earth, whose heat has grown fierce in the season of summer.
t.7.85: Urged by her steadfast husband, so pleasing to behold, to look upon the pole star, she lifted her face and, her throat choked with shyness, somehow managed to say, "It is seen."
t.7.86: Thus, when the marriage rite of taking the hand had been performed for them by the family priest learned in ritual, those two, the parents of all creatures, bowed to the Grandsire seated upon his lotus throne.
t.7.87: The bride was greeted by the Creator with the words, "Auspicious one, become the mother of a hero!" But he, though he was the Lord of Speech, fell motionless in thought over what blessing to bestow on the Eight-Formed One.
t.7.88: Afterwards the wife and husband came to the four-cornered altar, where all the ceremonial offerings had been arranged, and, seated on golden seats, they underwent the customary and longed-for rite of being showered with moist unbroken grains of rice.
t.7.89: Over the two of them Lakṣmī held up a lotus as a parasol, its long stalk serving as the handle; with the clusters of water drops clinging to the edges of its petals, it took on the beauty of a net of pearls drawn across it.
t.7.90: And Sarasvatī praised that couple with speech employed in two ways: the most excellent bridegroom with language purified by refinement, and the bride with language whose composition was easy to grasp.
t.7.91: For a while the two watched the apsarases' first performance, graceful in its dance movements, in which the different dramatic styles were made clear at the junctures of the plot and the melodies were matched to each change of rasa.
t.7.92: At the end of that, the gods, falling prostrate with hands joined in reverence against their crowns, begged Hara, who had now taken a wife, to accept the service of Pañcaśara, who had regained his bodily form at the end of the curse.
t.7.93: The Lord, his anger gone, allowed the working of his arrows even upon himself; for a request made at the right moment by those who know their purpose surely succeeds with masters.
t.7.94: Then the moon-crested god, having dismissed those hosts of deities, took the daughter of the lord of mountains by the hand and went to the bridal chamber, which was graced with the splendour of golden jars and protective auspicious ornaments, and where a bed had been laid out upon the ground.
t.7.95: There Īśa, by means of the comic grimaces of the Pramathas, secretly made Gaurī laugh: she whose only ornament was the shyness of a new bride, who turned her face away whenever he lifted it, and who could scarcely bring herself to speak even to the friends attending her bedchamber.
